relationship_to_restored_text: Interpretive contemplative layer aligned by verse. This does not replace the source-audited restored translation.

verses.mystical_translation: People begin joining David while he is still a fugitive at Ziklag.
Even Saul's Benjaminite relatives bring skill to David's camp.
The first supporters are named rather than absorbed into a faceless army.
More commanders and local identities enter the refuge force.
The list continues through five more warriors.
Korahite supporters are remembered.
Two sons of Jeroham complete the first group.
Gadite fighters are praised through animal imagery and wilderness competence.
Ezer, Obadiah, and Eliab lead the order.
Mishmannah and Jeremiah follow.
Attai and Eliel follow.
Johanan and Elzabad follow.
Jeremiah and Machbannai close the eleven.
The army ranks them by command size.
Their river crossing becomes a story of courage, while people in the valleys flee.
Benjamin and Judah send another delegation.
David asks for peace and fears betrayal, though his claim of clean hands remains open to scrutiny.
Amasai speaks peace and allegiance under the spirit's force, and David turns newcomers into commanders.
Manassites join after Philistine leaders refuse to trust David's divided position.
Seven commanders cross into David's camp at Ziklag.
They fight raiders and become leaders in the growing army.
Daily arrivals turn a fugitive band into a great camp.
Hebron becomes the gathering point for transferring Saul's kingdom.
Judah arrives with thousands prepared for war.
Simeon arrives with thousands.
Levi also enters the military count.
Aaronite leadership is counted in armed strength.
Young Zadok and his household commanders are praised for valor.
Benjamin's smaller delegation reveals continuing loyalty to Saul's house.
Ephraim's renowned warriors are counted.
Manasseh sends named representatives to make David king.
Issachar contributes political discernment about the moment.
Zebulun is praised for discipline and undivided loyalty.
Naphtali's commanders and troops are counted.
Dan's trained fighters are counted.
Asher's battle-ready people are counted.
The eastern tribes contribute the largest armed force.
The narrator imagines one-hearted unity around David, though real communities contain dissent and fear.
Three days of food and drink turn political transfer into shared table.
Farmers, bakers, transporters, animals, and neighboring households make national joy materially possible.

contemplative_note: The chapter celebrates unity, but unity is assembled from defectors, divided loyalties, armed tribes, political discernment, and enormous food logistics. The deepest sign of common life may not be the weapons kept in rank, but the bread, figs, oil, animals, and labor that let strangers eat together for three days.
